content: The speed of light in a vacuum, denoted by the symbol c, is a fundamental physical constant. It represents the velocity at which all electromagnetic radiation, including visible light, propagates in free space. This speed is also the maximum velocity at which any entity with zero rest mass can travel. In the International System of Units (SI), the speed of light in a vacuum is precisely defined as 299,792,458 meters per second (approximately 1,079,252,849 kilometers per hour). This exact value is a result of the definition of the meter, which, since October 21, 1983, has been based on the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second. Consequently, any improvement in the precision of measuring the speed of light would refine the definition of the meter without altering the numerical value of c. When light passes through a transparent or translucent medium, such as glass or air, its speed is reduced compared to its velocity in a vacuum. The ratio of the speed of light in a vacuum to its observed phase velocity in a medium is termed the refractive index of that medium. This phenomenon is responsible for effects such as refraction and dispersion, where light of different frequencies travels at varying speeds through the same material. In the framework of general relativity, the speed of light remains a critical constant of spacetime. However, the concepts of distance, time, and speed can become ambiguous due to the curvature of spacetime caused by gravitational effects. Locally, light in a vacuum always travels at the speed c relative to an observer. The constancy of the speed of light in a vacuum is a cornerstone of modern physics and forms the basis of Einstein's theory of special relativity. This principle, combined with the equivalence of all inertial reference frames, underpins the theory. Experimental evidence has consistently demonstrated that the speed of light is independent of the motion of its source. Furthermore, the two-way speed of light (e.g., from a source to a mirror and back) is constant, although measuring the one-way speed of light requires a convention for synchronizing clocks at the source and receiver. Einstein postulated that the speed of light should be taken as constant in all cases, whether one-way or two-way. It is important to note that it is the constant speed c, rather than light itself, that is fundamental to special relativity. Manipulating light to travel at speeds less than c does not directly affect the theory. Observers moving at high velocities experience distortions in distances and times according to Lorentz transformations, but these transformations preserve the constancy of the speed of light. The symbol c is widely used to denote the speed of light, derived from the Latin word celeritas, meaning swiftness. In some contexts, c₀ is used to specify the speed of light in a vacuum. In physics disciplines where the speed of light plays a significant role, such as relativity, it is common to use unit systems where c is normalized to 1, eliminating the need for a specific symbol. The finite speed of light has profound implications for causality and information transfer. If information could travel faster than c, causality would be violated, as effects could precede their causes in certain reference frames. This has never been observed. Information propagates within regions defined by a light cone, ensuring that causal relationships are preserved. The speed of light also affects practical applications, such as communications and navigation systems like GPS. In optical fibers, the speed of light is reduced by approximately 30% due to the medium's refractive index. This reduction, combined with signal delays caused by electronic switches and regenerators, impacts global communication systems. In space communications, the finite speed of light introduces noticeable delays, especially over large distances, as seen during the Apollo 8 mission to the Moon. These delays are also fundamental to the operation of GPS, where precise timing and synchronization of atomic clocks on satellites are required. In supercomputers, the speed of light imposes a limit on data transfer between processors. As clock frequencies increase, the finite speed of light becomes a limiting factor for the internal design of single chips, necessitating close placement of processors to minimize communication latencies. The speed of light is constant in all inertial reference frames, as demonstrated by Einstein's velocity addition formula. This formula ensures that no object can exceed the speed of light relative to another observer, establishing c as a universal speed limit in special relativity. Historically, the concept of the luminiferous aether was proposed as a medium through which light propagates, analogous to air for sound. However, the Michelson-Morley experiment failed to detect the Earth's motion through this hypothetical aether, leading to its discreditation and the development of special relativity. When light interacts with transparent materials, its observed speed can differ from c. The refractive index, defined as the ratio of c to the phase velocity of light in the material, determines this reduction. Denser media, such as water and glass, slow light significantly, with diamond reducing its speed to less than half of c. This slowing is responsible for phenomena like refraction and dispersion. In quantum mechanics, certain effects, such as quantum entanglement, may appear to involve faster-than-light interactions. However, these effects do not allow information transfer at speeds exceeding c, preserving causality. Similarly, phenomena like Čerenkov radiation occur when charged particles exceed the speed of light in a medium, analogous to a sonic boom. The speed of light has been a subject of scientific inquiry for centuries. Early experiments, such as those by Galileo and the Accademia del Cimento, attempted to measure its speed but were limited by the technology of the time. Modern measurements have refined our understanding of this fundamental constant, which remains central to both theoretical and applied physics.
